situation.text: You go to a house party in the USA. You meet the host, bring a dish, talk to the people and leave politely.

pages.goal: By the end of the class you can arrive at a party, greet the host, offer to bring something, ask a simple question and say goodbye politely.

Offer or ask: Can I bring…?
Ask an easy question about the house or the party

pages.title: Cultural snapshot — House parties in the USA
pages.intro: In the USA, a house party often has simple rules that nobody says out loud: bring something, ask before you do something and say thanks. Look and guess before you read.

cards.note: At a potluck, each guest brings a dish to share. The host usually tells you in the invitation.
In many homes people take their shoes off at the door. It is polite to ask: “Should I take my shoes off?”
For a dinner, arrive on time. For a casual party, a little late is often okay. If in doubt, ask the host.

levels.A2: Each guest brings a dish to share with everyone.
levels.B1: At a potluck, the party is a shared meal: everyone contributes a dish.
levels.B2: A potluck spreads the work and the cost: guests bring dishes, and the table becomes a mix of home cooking.

qs.q: Why do guests ask “Should I take my shoes off?”
qs.pt: Por que perguntar “Should I take my shoes off?”?

levels.A2: In some homes people do not wear shoes inside.
levels.B1: Some hosts prefer shoes off, and asking shows respect for the house.
levels.B2: Customs differ from home to home, so a quick question avoids awkward moments and shows respect.

qs.q: What is a polite way to leave a party?
qs.pt: Qual é uma forma educada de sair de uma festa?

levels.A2: Say thanks and give a reason: “I’d better go.”
levels.B1: Thank the host, say you had fun and give a short reason before you leave.
levels.B2: A warm thanks plus a light reason (“early day tomorrow”) lets you leave without seeming to dislike the party.

pages.compare: In Brazil guests often arrive later and bring drinks or dessert. In the USA people also bring something, but they often ask the host first. What would you bring to a friend’s party?

pages.title: Pronunciation lab — natural American English
pages.tip: In American English, the “t” between vowels often sounds like a quick “d”: “better” sounds like “beddy”, “party” like “par-dy”.

own.criteria: Say it twice. Did the “t” sound like a quick “d”?

teach.goal: UM só fenômeno: The American flap T.
solo: 3 passagens: escutar e identificar → reproduzir ritmo e entonação → usar em frase com conteúdo próprio.
Modele devagar e normal; peça que o estudante bata palmas na sílaba forte.
group: Coro, depois duplas; circule ouvindo.
Cada estudante cria uma frase própria.

pages.title: Level up — the same situation from A1 to C2
pages.intro: You do not need six different methods: the structure stays, while language complexity and autonomy grow.

ladder.goal: Arrive and offer food with short phrases.

ladder.say: Hi! Thanks for having me. Can I bring this cake to the kitchen?
Thanks so much for inviting me. I hope it’s okay that I brought some dessert.
It’s really kind of you to have us over. I took the liberty of bringing a little something for the table.
I hope you don’t mind, but I couldn’t arrive empty-handed, so I brought a little something to share.
It was good of you to have us; I’d hate to turn up without at least a small token of thanks.

pages.note: This progression is illustrative: complex sentences do not define a level on their own. CEFR also considers comprehension, autonomy, fluency, accuracy, interaction and appropriateness.
